Researchers offered a coin flip: Heads win $110, Tails lose $100. Most people say NO — even though it’s a good bet on average!

This bias explains why investors hold losing stocks, why sellers overprice houses, and why we hate risk.

0aC4_wTstno.description:
Random Number Tricks Your Brain! 😱
A totally random number can secretly control your guesses — this is the Anchoring Bias!
Researchers spin a wheel (1–100), then ask: “What % of African countries are in the UN?”
High number = people guess 60%. Low number = people guess 25%. Real answer? Only ~30%!
The wheel anchored their brain. This happens in prices, salaries, negotiations — everywhere!

UfQZhJjsYDw.description:
Paid $100 Ticket But Sick? Still Go! 😱

Economists say ignore money already spent… but this experiment proves we can’t!

You paid $100 for a concert ticket, then you get sick. Most people STILL go just so they don’t “waste” the money — even though it’s already gone!

This is the Sunk Cost Fallacy. It explains why we finish bad movies, stay in bad jobs, and keep bad relationships.

Free Mug? Now You Won’t Sell It Cheap! 😱

The famous Endowment Effect experiment proves we’re NOT rational with money!

Researchers gave people a free coffee mug… then asked how much they’d sell it for. Owners demanded $7!

But people without the mug only offered $3 to buy it. Same exact mug — value doubled just by owning it!

This explains why you refuse to sell your old phone or clothes cheap. We overvalue what we own!

Would You Reject FREE Money? 😱

The famous Ultimatum Game proves economists are wrong — humans are NOT rational!

Player 1 gets $10 to split. Player 2 can accept or reject. Reject = both get $0.

Watch what happens when someone offers only $1… most people REJECT it! They’d rather lose everything than feel cheated.

This experiment shows we value FAIRNESS more than cash. It explains real-life negotiations, salaries, and why fair deals matter!

Why do teams end up grinding overtime—even when no one wants to?
This 45‑second explainer shows how the Prisoner’s Dilemma maps onto overtime culture (a.k.a. the rat race or “involution”). We model two coworkers choosing between normal hours and overtime, walk through the four cases, and show why overtime becomes the dominant strategy: it looks individually safer no matter what the other person does—yet it leaves everyone worse off.

- The 2×2 payoff matrix for Normal vs Overtime
- Why dominant strategies can lead to bad group outcomes
- Why “doing more” can trap teams in burnout without real gains
